target: AG1's claim that a national-holiday Election Day would remove scheduling barriers and give people practical time to vote.
objection: Federal law does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off for a federal holiday, so many hourly retail and service workers would still be working and would not reliably gain time to vote.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday would materially reduce Election Day scheduling barriers for most eligible voters.
objection: If workers still have to work, the work/school scheduling barriers remain for them, so a holiday does not eliminate the practical constraint it is supposed to address.

target: AG1's implication that a national holiday would be broadly fair to all voters.
objection: Because low-income workers are more likely to rely on hourly service or retail jobs and cannot easily take unpaid time off, a holiday would disproportionately leave them with the same time-and-wage constraints rather than helping them.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday is an effective way to increase turnout.
objection: Research shows that making Election Day a holiday, by itself, is not an effective strategy for increasing voter turnout compared with other voting access reforms.

target: AG1's broader argument that a holiday is the best response to voting barriers.
objection: State-level reforms that directly require employer time off for voting, or automatic voter registration, are more reliable ways to remove the actual barriers that stop people from voting than a federal holiday.

target: AG2's claim that scheduling barriers remain because many workers would still have to work and therefore would not get practical time to vote.
objection: Even if some employers still schedule work, a holiday can still reduce the time-and-wage burden by making it more likely that employees get a day off, paid time, or shift flexibility, which makes voting feasible during polling hours.

target: AG1's argument that a holiday complements administrative reforms and therefore should still be adopted.
objection: A holiday does not, by itself, change polling hours or extend the voting window, so it does not reliably solve the actual time constraint faced by voters whose work schedules overlap fixed polling hours.

target: AG2's claim that unchanged polling hours mean a holiday cannot improve access.
objection: The relevant barrier is the time-and-wage penalty of leaving work, not the length of polling hours; if holiday designation reduces that penalty, more workers can realistically be present during the existing polling window.

target: AG1's claim that schools closing on a holiday will reduce caregiving burdens for parents.
objection: School closures do not necessarily solve childcare problems, because parents may still need replacement care and federal holiday status does not provide that care or guarantee paid time off from work.

target: AG2's claim that school closures do not help caregivers because they still need childcare.
objection: For many parents, school is the default daytime childcare provider, so if schools close on Election Day, they may not need to arrange additional paid or out-of-pocket coverage, which directly reduces the caregiving burden.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday fails because it does not itself provide childcare.
objection: Perceived civic importance and motivation can also drive constrained caregivers to arrange coverage or adjust schedules, so framing Election Day as a holiday can increase turnout even without direct childcare subsidies.

target: AG1's claim that the holiday meaningfully addresses school-related caregiving barriers for parents.
objection: For parents in hourly or shift jobs, school closures only help if they can actually be free during polling hours; if they still must work to avoid lost wages, the holiday does not remove the practical barrier to voting.

target: AG1's claim that school closures from a holiday reliably help caregivers vote.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off or schedule flexibility, so hourly retail and service workers may still have to work even when schools are closed.

target: AG1's implication that the holiday would ease the burden on low-income caregivers.
objection: Because low-income workers are more likely to be in hourly service or retail jobs and less able to absorb lost wages, holiday-induced school closures can leave the biggest constraints in place for them rather than reliably improving access.
